record.paper_title: A Nonequilibrium Statistical Ensemble Formalism. Maxent-Nesom: Concepts, Construction, Application, Open Questions and Criticisms
record.context_brief: explanatory basis of equilibrium probability assignments
record.original_question: Why do probabilistic assumptions based on equilibrium statistical mechanics work so well for predicting equilibrium measured values, if those probability distributions are justified by systematic inductive reasoning and the Principle of Indifference rather than by direct empirical frequencies over microscopic states?

evidence.quote: Therefore, there remains the explanatory question: Why do our probabilistic assumptions work so well in giving us equilibrium values?

Jaynes' prescription was to choose the probability distribution which maximizes the statistical entropy (now thought in the information-theoretic vein) relative to the known macroscopic constraints, using the standard measure over the phase space to characterize the space of possibilities.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a classical Hamiltonian system with phase space $\Gamma$ equipped with the Liouville measure $d\mu$. For a macroscopic system in equilibrium, one is given a finite collection of macroscopic constraints in the form of expectation values $\langle F_i\rangle = f_i$ for observables $F_i:\Gamma\to\mathbb{R}$, $i=1,\dots,n$. The MaxEnt (Jaynes) prescription assigns to the system the probability density $\rho^\star$ on $\Gamma$ that maximizes the Gibbs–Shannon entropy 
$$S[\rho] = -\int_\Gamma \rho(x)\log\rho(x)\,d\mu(x)$$
subject to the normalization $\int\rho\,d\mu = 1$ and the constraints $\int F_i\,\rho\,d\mu = f_i$. This prescription is justified a priori by an inductive principle (the Principle of Indifference / maximum noncommittal inference) rather than by empirically measured frequencies over microscopic states.

Provide a rigorous explanation, within a precise mathematical framework (e.g., ergodic theory, large deviations, concentration of measure on high-dimensional energy surfaces, or typicality theorems), of why the equilibrium expectation values $\int G\,\rho^\star\,d\mu$ computed via this inductive MaxEnt assignment agree, to excellent accuracy, with the time-averaged values $\lim_{T\to\infty}\tfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T G(\Phi_t x)\,dt$ measured for typical initial conditions $x$ under the Hamiltonian flow $\Phi_t$, for macroscopic observables $G$. In particular, identify mathematical conditions on the system (dimension, interactions, observables) under which the inductively justified MaxEnt distribution can be proved to reproduce empirical equilibrium frequencies.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a long-standing foundational question on the justification of equilibrium statistical mechanics (the "explanatory question" behind Jaynes' MaxEnt and the Principle of Indifference). Partial mathematical answers exist via ergodic theory, large deviations, and typicality/concentration-of-measure results (Lanford, Goldstein, Lebowitz, and others), but no universally accepted complete derivation exists; the problem remains open as a foundational issue.

status_evidence.title: Boltzmann's Approach to Statistical Mechanics
status_evidence.snippet: Goldstein discusses typicality and why equilibrium probabilities work, noting it remains a foundational issue.
status_evidence.claim: Foundational status of why MaxEnt/equilibrium probabilities reproduce measurements is still debated.

status_evidence.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Philosophy of Statistical Mechanics
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews competing justifications (ergodic, typicality, Jaynesian inductive) and notes no consensus.
status_evidence.claim: The explanatory question remains open in foundations of statistical mechanics.
